bandi.titolo: New European Bauhaus Prizes — Rising Stars
bandi.sottotitolo: Strand B — for talents aged 30 or under
bandi.descrizione: The European Commission's prize for people who make the green transition beautiful, not only efficient. Strand B is reserved for authors aged 30 or under.
bandi.premioNota: per each winning category · €5,000 for runners-up
bandi.scadenzaNota: Dates from the previous edition — check the official site before applying
vantaggi: Communication package from the European Commission

categorie.nome: Arts, culture and heritage as drivers of change

descrizioneLunga: **Strand B is reserved for you.** Every listed author must be __30 years old or younger__ on the closing day. You are not competing against architecture firms or city councils - you compete against other young people with an idea.

An entry does not have to be finished. Concepts are accepted __at any stage__, from a plan on paper to a working prototype. What the jury looks for is whether the idea is **sustainable, beautiful and inclusive at once** - two out of three is not enough, and that is the hard part.
Winning brings EUR 15,000, a communication package from the Commission, a mentoring programme, and a __public vote across Europe__ that puts the project in front of thousands of people.

vincitori.sintesi: Mushroom roots turned into a building material. Agricultural and textile waste becomes a mycelium skin for urban structures in Lisbon.
vincitori.esteso: Mycelium — the root network of a mushroom — will bind almost anything it is fed. The team fed it agricultural and textile waste from around Lisbon and grew it into panels: a skin for urban structures that is made from what the city throws away and returns to the ground when it is done. It won in the Rising Stars strand, which is the one reserved for people aged 30 or under. Worth remembering when the idea feels too small: this was a material, grown in a room.

vincitori.sintesi: Cluj's green lung: a large forest park managed so that people can use it and the forest survives being used.
vincitori.esteso: Cluj-Napoca has a forest on its doorstep and, like most cities with one, was slowly wearing it out. The project is a large forest park managed on an uncomfortable principle: that people must be able to use it **and** the forest must survive being used. That means deciding where the paths go, what gets closed, and who says so — governance work, not landscape work, and the reason it won under “reconnecting with nature” rather than under design.

vincitori.sintesi: One thousand fountains, mapped. Sarajevo's public water points found, documented and brought back into use with the people who drink from them.
vincitori.esteso: Sarajevo has around a thousand public fountains. Nobody had a list. The team found them, documented them, and put them back into use — with the people who actually drink from them, not on their behalf. It took the public vote, which is the prize decided by everyone across Europe rather than by a jury, and that is telling: it is the kind of project whose value is obvious to anyone who has ever looked for a drink of water.

vincitori.sintesi: Empty spaces opened for free: community kitchens, family areas, greening, run with the people who need them most.
vincitori.esteso: Empty buildings and unused lots, opened for free: community kitchens, spaces for families, planting. The organisation runs them with the people who need them most rather than for them, which is slower and is the whole point. A runner-up in the awards, and the most directly copyable thing on this page — every one of our eight cities has a building standing empty right now.

vincitori.sintesi: Ordinary street signage redesigned to host pollinators - the poles and panels a city already owns, turned into habitat.
vincitori.esteso: A city already owns thousands of poles and panels: street signs, posts, brackets. Pollino redesigns that ordinary furniture to host pollinators. No new land, no new budget line, no permission to acquire anything — just a different specification for something that was going to be installed anyway. It won under “reconnecting with nature” in 2025, and it is the clearest example on this page of an idea that is small on purpose.

vincitori.sintesi: Students and residents designed a shared courtyard together, built from construction material recovered in the neighbourhood.
vincitori.esteso: Students and residents designed a shared courtyard together — actually together, in the same room, over months — and then built it from construction material recovered in the neighbourhood. It won under local democracy rather than under design, and that is the honest classification: the courtyard is the visible part, the process of agreeing on it was the work.

bandi.occhiello: Turn an idea into something Europe pays for.
bandi.vincitoriNota: Progetti realmente premiati dalla Commissione europea.

bandi.sottotitolo: A group of young people, funded directly — no organisation needed
bandi.occhiello: Five of you. One local problem. European money.
bandi.descrizione: A group of at least five young people applies on its own, without going through any organisation, to run a project in their own community for up to twelve months.
bandi.scadenzaNota: Deadlines from the current programme guide — check the National Agency before applying
bandi.etaNota: years old · group of 5 or more
vantaggi: A coach assigned to the group
Runs in your own town, not abroad
descrizioneLunga: **This is the one call you can win without an institution behind you.** Five young people aged __18 to 30__, legally resident in the same country, register the group and apply directly. No university signature, no partner NGO, no co-funding.
The project must address __a real need in your own community__ and last between two and twelve months. The Commission funds the running costs, and assigns you a coach if you ask for one.
The 2026 call for the European Solidarity Corps carries a budget of **over €129 million** across all its strands. Solidarity Projects are the smallest and by far the least competitive door into it.
bandi.vincitoriNota: Questo non è un concorso: non esiste un elenco di vincitori perché non c’è una graduatoria. È un contributo che si ottiene se si è in regola con i requisiti. Le tre schede qui sotto spiegano come funziona, e sono scritte da noi.

vincitori.sintesi: This is a grant, not a prize. You are not competing against other groups: you are being checked against a list of requirements.
vincitori.esteso: Every other call on this page has winners because it has losers. This one does not work that way. The National Agency assesses your application against published criteria — relevance, quality of the plan, impact on your community — and funds it if it clears the bar. Two good applications from the same town can both succeed. That changes what you should spend your time on: not on being more impressive than someone else, but on being unambiguously eligible.

vincitori.titolo: Five of you, and nobody above you
vincitori.sintesi: At least five young people aged 18 to 30, legally resident in the same country. No university, no NGO, no co-funding.
vincitori.esteso: The group registers itself and applies directly. There is no host organisation to find, no institutional signature to chase, and no matching funds to raise — which is precisely what stops most student ideas before they start. One of you takes on the legal representation of the group; if you would rather not, an organisation can hold the money for you without taking over the project. A coach is available if you ask for one.

vincitori.titolo: Two to twelve months, €500 a month
vincitori.sintesi: Up to €500 a month for project management, for a project lasting between two and twelve months, in your own community.
vincitori.esteso: The contribution covers running the thing: preparation, carrying out the activities, evaluating them, and telling people about them afterwards. It is deliberately modest, and it is meant for a project that happens where you already live — rural, isolated or marginalised communities are explicitly favoured. Twelve months at €500 is €6,000, which is not a salary and is not supposed to be: it is enough to stop a good idea from dying of small expenses.

bandi.guidaEtichetta: How to apply as a group

bandi.sottotitolo: One winning project per country, then one for Europe
bandi.occhiello: Win at home first. Then compete for Europe.
bandi.descrizione: The European Parliament and the Charlemagne Prize Foundation award projects that build a shared European identity. One national winner per Member State, then a European first prize.
bandi.scadenzaNota: Deadline is usually early February — confirm on the Parliament site
vantaggi: A national win even if you do not take Europe
descrizioneLunga: **There are two competitions here, not one.** Every Member State picks __its own national winner__ — so you are first judged against projects from your country, not against all of Europe. Twenty-seven projects then go forward to the European jury.

Entries must be run by people aged __16 to 30__ and must promote European and international understanding, shared identity, or practical cooperation across borders. A project already running counts; it does not have to be new.

The three European winners receive **€7,500, €5,000 and €2,500**, and all national winners are invited to the ceremony in **Aachen** — the same city, and the same week, as the Charlemagne Prize itself.

vincitori.sintesi: A pan-European media outlet run by young people: articles, podcasts, TikTok videos and interviews, all asking what a European identity actually is.
vincitori.esteso: Forum Europaeum took the first prize of the 2025 edition. It is not an app and not an event — it is a publication, made by young people across several countries, that treats European identity as a question worth arguing about rather than a slogan. It works in the formats its readers already use: long articles for those who want them, podcasts for the commute, TikTok for everyone else. The jury rewarded the fact that it had been running long enough to have an audience, not just a plan.

vincitori.sintesi: “Thanks that we can vote” — a campaign to get 18-to-29-year-olds to the polls in the 2024 European elections.
vincitori.esteso: Turnout among young Czech voters was the problem, and the team treated it as one: not a poster campaign, but education and outreach aimed squarely at people who had decided in advance that the European Parliament had nothing to do with them. The name is a deliberate provocation — a reminder, in a country whose grandparents could not vote freely, that the right is recent. It took second prize and €5,000.

vincitori.sintesi: Free legal support for people facing gender-based discrimination and sexualised violence, run by law students.
vincitori.esteso: Law students giving free legal advice to the people least able to pay for it: women and members of the LGBTIQ+ community facing discrimination, sexualised violence, or simply a legal situation nobody had explained to them. It is the smallest of the three prizes and the most directly useful — a service that exists on the days it opens, whether or not anyone writes about it. Third prize, €2,500.

bandi.sottotitolo: Three days, ten countries, EU space data
bandi.occhiello: A weekend. Ten cities. Real satellite data.
bandi.descrizione: The EU space programme opens Galileo and Copernicus data to teams who build something with it over a single weekend, in ten countries at once.
bandi.premioNota: to each of three winning teams · plus 100 hours of mentoring
vantaggi: Free access to Galileo and Copernicus data
Six months of mentoring for the winners
descrizioneLunga: **This is the fastest one on the list.** It takes __a single weekend__, not a year. You arrive with a team, or you form one on the first evening, and you leave on Sunday with something that runs.

The material is __EU space data__: Galileo positioning and Copernicus Earth observation, opened for the event with the tools to use them. Previous editions have run on agriculture, defence, mobility and climate resilience.

The 12th edition runs **27–29 November 2026 in ten countries at once** — among them Bulgaria, Germany, Italy, Lithuania and Poland, which is five of our eight cities. Prizes are €5,000, €3,000 and €1,000, plus **six months of mentoring**.

vincitori.sintesi: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data read for fresh snowfall, crossed with live weather, to give the probability of an avalanche where you are standing.
vincitori.esteso: Built over one weekend by a team from Bulgaria. Copernicus satellites pass over the mountains anyway; the team used Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 to detect how much snow has just fallen, then crossed that with live weather data to produce a probability for a specific point — not a regional bulletin, but the slope you are about to cross. It won the 10th edition and €3,000, plus a hundred hours of mentoring to keep going.

vincitori.sintesi: Galileo and Copernicus data tracking athletes during a race, so spectators can follow them on a live map or through an augmented-reality camera.
vincitori.esteso: A trail race disappears into the forest and the spectators lose it for hours. TrailRadar uses Galileo positioning and Copernicus terrain data to keep every runner on a live map, and adds an augmented-reality camera view: point the phone at the hillside and see who is on it. The team came out of the Finnish edition and went on to the Aalto Startup Center. Same weekend, same €3,000, same hundred hours.

vincitori.sintesi: Paragliding safety in AR glasses: wind patterns, landing zones, restricted airspace and proximity alerts, in the pilot’s field of view.
vincitori.esteso: Paragliders make decisions with their hands full and their eyes on the horizon. GlideBuddy puts what they need into AR glasses — wind patterns, where it is safe to land, which airspace is closed, and sensor-based alerts when something else is too close. Weather and terrain analysis from EU space data, built in three days by an Italian team, third of the three winners of the 10th edition.

squadre.sintesi: Eight campuses throw away the same chairs, lamps and lab stools every June, and buy them again in September. We are mapping what leaves each building and building a shared board where it finds a second owner across the alliance.
squadre.cerca: Someone who can build a simple web catalogue, and one person per campus to do the counting.

squadre.sintesi: A portable wooden structure that sits in a town square for a week and records what residents actually want from the university next door. Built once, shipped between four cities, transcribed and published openly.
squadre.cerca: A carpenter or product designer, and someone comfortable with audio editing.

squadre.sintesi: Student housing built in the 1960s is being demolished across Europe without anyone photographing it. We document four buildings before they go, with the people who lived in them, and turn it into a travelling exhibition.
squadre.cerca: A photographer, and someone who can handle archive permissions.

squadre.sintesi: Every student project starts from zero: the same budget template, the same permission letters, the same mistakes. We are collecting what previous funded teams actually used and releasing it as an open toolkit anyone in Europe can copy.
squadre.cerca: Someone who has already run a funded project, and a translator for at least one more language.
